issues.failure_explanation: The derivation of \|E\|_\infty \le 1.1(b-a) replaces the discrete sum h\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z} g(jh), g(s)=(\pi/2)\cosh s/\cosh^2((\pi/2)\sinh s), by the integral \int g\,ds = 2 using an approximate equality "\simeq", inside a chain of inequalities. No trapezoidal/DE quadrature error estimate is given, so the sign and size of the discrepancy are uncontrolled; the inequality does not follow as a rigorous statement. Since eq:Ebound feeds eq:ImEinvNorm and Theorem 3.2, the theorem's stated clean inequality "\le" is not established as written.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add a rigorous bound for the sum, e.g., the standard estimate for the unimodal integrand h\sum_j g(jh) \le \int g + 2h\|g\|_\infty = 2 + \pi h (or a DE-trapezoid error bound), yielding \|E\|_\infty \le 1.1(b-a)(1+\pi h/2); tighten the hypothesis to 1.1L(b-a)(1+\pi h/2) < 1 and propagate the (1+O(h)) factor into \eqref{eq:MGSNorm2} and the sample computation.
issues.overall_effect: Theorem 3.2's bound \eqref{eq:MGSNorm2} (the paper's central convergence-factor estimate), the numerical sample bound 0.06197, and the rough estimate w \lesssim 1.1(b-a) used to motivate Assumption 3.1 all rest on an uncontrolled approximation; as stated, the theorem's inequality is unsupported, although the true quadrature error is small so a slightly adjusted statement is expected to survive.
issues.title: Uncontrolled "\simeq" (trapezoidal sum replaced by integral) inside the proof of Theorem 3.2's rigorous bound
issues.why_classification: The repair requires a genuinely missing (though contained and standard) analytic lemma and slightly modifies the theorem's hypothesis and constants, which is more than a local fix; but the conclusion, the O((log N)^2/N) rate, and the advertised scope all survive, so no new global architecture or major loss is involved.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: the DE transformation \eqref{eq:DE} is replaced by the identity transformation $\varphi(s)=s$ and $p_j(s)$ is a piecewise linear function with $p_j(s_i)=\delta_{ij}$

issues.failure_explanation: With \varphi(s)=s and piecewise-linear hat functions p_j, the weights P_j(s_i)=\int_a^{s_i}p_j ds' equal h for j \le i-1 and h/2 for j=i (interior nodes), so the scheme reads \tilde x_i - \tilde x_{i-1} = (h/2)(f(t_{i-1},\tilde x_{i-1}) + f(t_i,\tilde x_i)), which is the implicit trapezoidal rule. Implicit Euler would require the increment to be h f(t_i,\tilde x_i) (piecewise-constant p_j). The identification is false; only the (correct) lower-triangularity/causality observation survives.

failure_location.quote: In fact, this method is nothing but the implicit Euler method and the lower triangularity means that the method respects causality

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace "implicit Euler method" with "implicit trapezoidal rule".
issues.overall_effect: Only this intuitive remark is wrong; no theorem, algorithm, or numerical claim depends on the identification.
issues.title: The fictitious lower-triangular method is the implicit trapezoidal rule, not the implicit Euler method
issues.why_classification: Isolated factual mislabel with a single forced correction; no substantive claim, method, rate, or guarantee is affected.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: we present some numerical examples that confirm the validity of Theorems \ref{Th3-1} and \ref{Th3-2}.
the constant $M$ can be chosen so that $w\le \frac{\rho}{M}$.
\caption{$\|M_{\rm GS}\|_{\infty}$ and its upper bound as a function of $N$ for Example 3.}

issues.failure_explanation: For Example 3 the interval is [0,1] (b-a=1). On the stated region with \rho=1/2: (a) M \ge \sup |f_1| = \sup|x_1 x_2| = (5/2)\cdot 1 = 5/2, while the paper's own estimate gives w \simeq 1.1(b-a) = 1.1, so Mw \approx 2.75 > 1/2 = \rho, violating Assumption 3.1(iii); no other \rho rescues this, since M \ge (2+\rho)(1/2+\rho) makes \rho \ge wM impossible. (b) The infinity-norm Lipschitz constant on the region is L = 7/2 (largest row sum of |J|, attained), so 1.1L(b-a) = 3.85 > 1, violating Theorem 3.2's hypothesis; with this L the bound \eqref{eq:MGSNorm2} has a negative denominator 1-1.1L(b-a) and cannot upper-bound \|M_{GS}\|_\infty \ge 0. Nevertheless the section presents Example 3 as one of the examples that "confirm the validity of Theorems 3.1 and 3.2" and Fig. Ex3-2 plots "\|M_{GS}\|_\infty and its upper bound". The example cannot validate either theorem and the plotted bound is unjustified.

failure_location.quote: In this case, if we choose $\rho=1/2$, $\mathcal{D}_{\rm rho}^{\prime}$ implies $x_1\in[3/2,5/2]$, $x_2\in[0,1]$ and $x_3\in[1,2]$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either shorten Example 3's interval to [0,b'] with b' satisfying w \le \rho/M and 1.1Lb' < 1 (e.g., b' \lesssim 1/8 with \rho=1/2, M=5/2, L=7/2) and redo the computations, or state explicitly that Example 3 lies outside the sufficient-condition regime and remove/relabel the "upper bound" curve and the framing sentence.
issues.overall_effect: Example 3 — the paper's only nonlinear test problem — provides no support for Theorem 3.1's sufficient condition or Theorem 3.2's convergence-factor bound; the section-level claim that the examples confirm the theorems is overstated, and the "upper bound" curve in Fig. Ex3-2 cannot be the bound from Theorem 3.2. Theorems 3.1/3.2 themselves and Examples 1-2 are unaffected.
issues.title: Example 3 violates Assumption 3.1(iii) and Theorem 3.2's condition 1.1L(b-a)<1, yet is presented as confirming Theorems 3.1 and 3.2
issues.why_classification: The main theorems survive untouched, but restoring the example's claimed role requires changing its regime and recomputation, or accepting a limited but real weakening of the numerical-validation claims (losing the only nonlinear confirmation of the bound); this exceeds a local fix without requiring new global proof architecture.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: For general $m$ and $A(0)$, the matrix exponential $\exp(tA(0))$ has to be calculated numerically.

issues.failure_explanation: For tridiagonal A(0) and m \ge 3, exp(tA(0)) is generically a dense m x m matrix, whose LR (LU) factors are full unit lower-triangular and upper-triangular matrices. A product of a unit lower-subdiagonal factor and an upper-bidiagonal factor is banded and cannot equal the dense matrix exp(tA(0)). Step (ii) of the stated general-m procedure is therefore impossible as described for m \ge 3; the description happens to be vacuously consistent only with the m=2 example actually computed. The procedure is valid only with full triangular factors.

failure_location.quote: Compute $\exp(tA(0))$ and its $LR$ decomposition $\exp(tA(0))=L_t R_t$, where $L_t$ is a unit lower subdiagonal matrix and $R_t$ is an upper bidiagonal matrix.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace "unit lower subdiagonal matrix" and "upper bidiagonal matrix" with "unit lower triangular matrix" and "upper triangular matrix".
issues.overall_effect: The general-m Toda solution procedure is mis-specified at step (ii); the paper's actual use is confined to m=2, where the description is accidentally correct, so the exact Lotka-Volterra solution used in Example 3 is unaffected.
issues.title: LR factors of exp(tA(0)) are full triangular matrices, not unit lower-subdiagonal and upper-bidiagonal, for general m
issues.why_classification: The correction is a two-term description fix; the intended standard factorization procedure is valid and all of the paper's computations (m=2) are unaffected, so no substantive claim or guarantee is lost.
